Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,.$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

- For $x=\frac{1}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$  So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14065827/assets/f518a206638071a7b8548882a453123b6d78aed0aa94cc0e6e23429f22c6f1b3.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [r]_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
